tfn.s: The review proved that 7,000 steps prevent illness.
tfn.why: The text says the study looked "rather than proving that one exact number prevents illness."

tfn.s: The 10,000-step idea became popular through a Japanese product.
tfn.why: The text says: "It became popular through a Japanese step-counting product sold in the 1960s."

tfn.s: Most watch owners reach 10,000 steps a day.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say how many watch owners reach 10,000 steps.

tfn.s: Step totals cannot show how hard somebody is working.
tfn.why: The text says step totals cannot show "how hard someone is working or whether they are getting stronger."

tfn.s: A person who walks fast for half an hour will always reach 10,000 steps.
tfn.why: The text says such a person may "still finish below 10,000."

focus.note: Think about what the link does: contrast, reason, result or condition.

items.s: The review ____ in July 2025 by The Lancet Public Health.

tfn.s: Somebody who goes from 2,000 to 4,000 steps a day may have made a meaningful change.
tfn.why: The text says this person "may be making a meaningful change even if the famous target remains out of reach."

tfn.s: The review shows that walking alone caused every difference in health.
tfn.why: The text says the studies "cannot establish that walking alone caused every difference."

tfn.s: Fitness watches will be updated to show the new target.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not mention any plan to update fitness watches.

tfn.s: A fixed target can discourage people who struggle with mobility.
tfn.why: The text says a number that motivates one person "can discourage another who struggles with mobility."

tfn.s: The review found the same benefits at 2,000 steps as at 7,000 steps.
tfn.why: The text links 7,000 rather than 2,000 steps with a "considerably lower risk of death."

focus.note: Some linkers go before a noun or -ing form, some join two clauses, and some start a new sentence after a full stop.

items.s: ____ being widely recognised, the number has no strong scientific basis.

A step counter suits some people, ____ it discourages others.
A target can be useful ____ it makes people feel like failures.
Few people realise how much distance they have ____ by the end of a long shift on their feet.
Constantly missing a daily target ____ confidence rather than building it.
The trial was delayed by an unexpected ____ with the way the devices recorded movement.
Participants who were already ____ of walking long distances may have been healthier from the start.
A ____ rise of 500 steps a day is easier to maintain than a sudden doubling.
Treating the screen as the ____ judge of a good walk ignores enjoyment.

decide that something is not possible

items.s: The headline figure invites ____ because the reduction in risk is relative.
A universal rule shows little ____ to differences in age and mobility.
Trackers can give a ____ impression of how hard someone is exercising.

tfn.s: The review found that the benefits stopped completely after 7,000 steps.
tfn.why: The text reports "diminishing returns beyond roughly 5,000 to 7,000 steps", which is not the same as no benefit.

tfn.s: Someone who is already active might gain from movement that a step target does not capture.
tfn.why: The text says "for somebody already active, further movement may offer benefits not captured by a universal daily rule."

tfn.s: The 47% figure compares people with two different daily step counts.
tfn.why: The text says it compares 7,000 steps with 2,000.

tfn.s: The authors recommend replacing step targets with activity minutes.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say whether the authors suggest activity minutes instead of steps.

tfn.s: Fewer than half of the 57 studies contributed to specific meta-analyses.
tfn.why: The text says 31 of the 57 contributed, which is more than half.

speak.title: Role-play: the step counter debate
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You have walked 8,000 steps today and you want to reach 10,000 before bed. Ask your friend to come for another walk. Explain why the number matters to you.

b.text: You have had a long day and you don't want another walk. You have read that 7,000 steps is already good. Give your reasons, then suggest a different plan.

phrases: I'd like to do another walk tonight.
That's not really necessary, is it?
The review says 7,000 is already good.
We're both tired, so why don't we go tomorrow?
Could we do a shorter walk instead?
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did you agree on a plan, and who gave the better reasons?
